items.title: Contravariance Theory, Part 4b: RSA Empirics
items.description: Let's look at a whole bunch of scatter plots.
items.content:
(This post is part of a series on Contravariance Theory. See Part 0 to get the big picture. This post is the data-driven companion to Part 4a: RSA Theory, a broader conceptual and mathematical discussion of RSA.)

Overview

The Part 4a: RSA Theory post has 4 predictions for the RSA-ridge relationship. Here, we illustrate them empirically:

  1. Ridge vs RSA: does the theoretically-predicted ridge-vs-RSA frontier formula hold, at least approximately?

  2. Predicting high-level behaviors: does the ridge metric of neural fit better predict metrics of human visual behavior patterns, as compared to the RSA metric of neural fit, as weak-strong equivalence results would suggest?

  3. Low-level visual phenomenology: which neural-fit metric better predicts V1 physiology metrics?

  4. Sampling issues: which neural-fit metric better aligns different data samples of the same modality and brain area?

1. Ridge vs RSA

Part 4a: RSA Theory told us that we expect an RSA-vs-ridge plot to look something like one of the below plots:

The left plot above obtains if the RSA is pretty close to “canonical” — e.g. not contaminated by task-irrelevant noise. The right is more like one would expect if task-irrelevant noise dominates.

How does RSA relate to ridge in practice? Let’s look at some plots. We’ll start with data from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD). Each panel below corresponds to one of the brain areas in the NSD localizer scheme. Each dot is a model, and the model zoo ranges over a wide set of distinct vision models.1 The x-axis of each plot is RSA similarity and the y-axis is Pearson’s r between data and the ridge-fit model predictions.2

To my eye, the NSD results seem pretty canonical, actually — fairly clean-looking.

Here are the results for the LAION-fMRI dataset — pretty similar looking:

Here is the same for the Bold Moments Dataset (BMD). Much the same pattern emerges, a bit less clean — a little more confounded than the NSD or LAION-fMRI results3:

And finally, here is the same for the Things Ventral-stream Spiking Dataset (TVSD):

Results in V1 and V4 look “kind of ok” in an absolute sense, but comparatively noisy in comparison to the fMRI cases, presumably due to the difficulty of obtaining a nonbiased sample with electrophysiology methods, especially in early visual areas.

Key implication for NeuroAI: The RSA/ridge relationship is pretty tight in many cases even without canonicalization, but is probably fairly susceptible to sampling incompleteness inherent in real neural samples.

2. Predicting high-level behaviors

Another prediction of the contravariance theory for RSA and ridge is that raw RSA will be less predictive of behavior across a wide variety of model implementations than ridge, because raw RSA doesn’t obey Zippering (e.g. control by downstream task) while linear similarity does. We can test this by plotting behavioral metrics against the same neural fit metrics as above.

Brain-Score implements a wide variety of behavioral metrics and has a strong model zoo, so it’s a good place to start. We are interested in asking: “To what extent does a model’s being brain-like, under one or another quantitative metric of brain-likeness, predict its behavioral consistency?” Thus we consider brain-likeness as assessed relative to several recent large-scale neural datasets, including NSD, TVSD, and the just-released LAION-fMRI dataset.

Behavioral consistency can be assessed by any of the “behavioral” metrics on Brain-Score. There are 43 individual (non-aggregate) behavioral metrics, and we consider them all. Each of these measures a model’s consistency with some pattern of human behavior, rather than its raw performance accuracy on some task. Each metric is based on comparing model error patterns to those measured in a real human psychophysical experiment on some task.

Here are the results of one, the Rajalingham-i2n metric, which tests the ability of a model to predict image-by-image human object-recognition confusion patterns across several thousand naturalistic images. The x-axis is model-to-human behavioral similarity according to this metric, the y-axis remains ridge-based neural similarity. Each row is a different neural dataset and each column is a different brain area (V1, V4, and IT).

We notice that the correlations are pretty decent from IT, and nontrivial but less good from V1. This is not a major surprise, since IT is thought to support object recognition behavior, but it’s good to see the intuition confirmed.

Now let’s have a look at the same Dependent Variables (DVs), but with different Independent Variables (IVs) — in this case, RSA similarity:

We only show NSD and LAION-fMRI comparisons here because Brain-Score doesn’t implement RSA for the TVSD dataset. But the conclusion is pretty clear: ridge tracks behavior substantially more accurately than (raw) RSA, despite ridge and RSA being decently correlated as shown in the last section. Attempting to predict behavioral similarity pulls RSA and ridge apart.

This pattern is not confined to the Rajalingham-i2n metric. Here are similar results for the Geirhos2021eidolonIII-error_consistency metric, which measures model error-pattern similarity to human choices in images with blurred object appearances but natural pixel distributions (see Fig. 12 in the Geirhos texture-bias paper). First from ridge:

Then from RSA:

The absolute correlations are lower (like ~0.65 from IT to the metric rather than ~0.85) but the ridge-RSA pattern remains the same.

In fact, taken across all the behavioral metrics in the Brain-Score collection, the pattern is extremely robust:

Breaking that out more finely, out of 172 metric / brain area combinations, RSA is more correlated to behavior than ridge in only 3 situations. This is summarized here:

Key implication for NeuroAI: Task-irrelevant symmetries have a meaningful effect on RSA’s ability to align neural predictivity with behavioral metrics, an issue that does not affect ridge similarity.

3. Low-level visual phenomenology

One might wonder if the ability of ridge to better predict measurement variables than RSA similarity is confined to “high-level” behaviors. To test this we consider the V1-Marques metrics in Brain-Score. These metrics were compiled from the literature on “classic” V1 physiology, and measure detailed single-neuron phenomenologies such as circular variance and texture selectivity. There are a total of 22 such metrics in Brain-Score.

Here are ridge-vs-metric results for texture selectivity in the Freeman-Ziemba V1/V2 dataset:

Overall absolute predictivities are not amazing numerically, but it’s hard to know exactly what the noise ceilings are (this is definitely a question for another time!). Relatively speaking, however, the pattern is maintained — predictivity drops substantially when we pass to RSA:

Looking across all areas and V1 metrics, we see the pattern robustly. For example, using the NSD dataset as the prediction signal, and looking across the main areas covered by Brain-Score we see:

We find that V1-Ridge results are meaningfully better than other areas and RSA at predicting low-level V1 physiology. And here is the summary result for predicting low-level V1 metrics from V1 neural predictivity metrics, over all the main datasets in Brain-Score that support this kind of comparison, including NSD V1, LAION-fMRI V1, Triple-N V1, and the underlying Freeman-Ziemba V1 data:

Again, while overall predictivities are not amazing4, ridge retains a meaningful edge over RSA for all datasets and essentially all metrics.

Why do we see all these results pointing in the same direction, whether they are “high-level behaviors” or low-level V1 physiology measures? We posit that the underlying cause of these observations is the contravariance theory consequence described in Part 4a: RSA Theory: that the task-linked core geometry component of RSA — and only that component — obeys weak-strong equivalence and zippering.

Key implication for NeuroAI: The pattern of ridge being a better predictor of other outcome DVs is not just confined to high-level behaviors, consistent with the generality of the underlying theoretical explanation for these results.

4. Sampling issues

One of the major issues discussed in Part 4a: RSA Theory is the fact that raw RSA is susceptible to sampling issues, essentially because sampling issues are the “measurement consequences” of the task-irrelevant symmetry nuisances identified in the Theiß et al paper.

The issue of sampling is especially pronounced in ephys datasets because of the nature of sampling, especially in older-school single-electrode datasets (such as the Freeman-Ziemba). It is thus instructive to compare the alignment of RSA and ridge on two different neural samples. In this case we compare the older Freeman-Ziemba V1 dataset against TVSD-V1. The Freeman-Ziemba V1 dataset consists of 105 single electrode sites tested on 315 oriented Gabor and texture stimuli, while the TVSD V1 dataset consists of 960 array electrode sites tested on approximately 22k natural images.

Under ridge we can see that these datasets are both measuring a common physical system (macaque V1) with a common methodology (electrophysiology); under raw RSA this is substantially obscured.

Key implication for NeuroAI: Sampling is a big problem for neuroscience.

1

In most of the plots shown in this post, we use Brain-Score as the source of data. However for the RSA-vs-ridge analysis we wanted to show areas other than just V1, V2, V4, and IT, and those are not accessible via Brain-Score. Thus we are using our own lab-internal model zoo for this purpose, courtesy of the work of Khaled Jedoui.

2

Specifically, for each neural unit (electrode site or voxel, depending on the dataset): (i) the ridge-fit predictions are extracted on held-out test images, (ii) Pearson’s r is computed for that unit; and (iii) the reported score is median predictivity over units in the indicated brain area.

3

And for BMD, which is a video dataset, the predictivities are worse relative to the noise ceilings than for the static image dataset. This is orthogonal I suppose to the topical issue of RSA-vs-ridge, but it indicates, perhaps unsurprisingly, that at least in some brain areas, standard vision models, which are mostly image-based, are not as good at predicting the neural responses to videos.

4

An interesting question for a future post…

items.title: Contravariance Theory, Part 4a: RSA theory
items.description: A tale of two metrics, or, coming to terms with symmetries.
items.content:
(This post is part of a series on Contravariance Theory. See Part 0 to get the big picture. This is a “theory-heavy” post — also see the companion Part 4b: RSA empirics for real data.)

There are many metrics NeuroAI people use for comparing neural network models to real brain data. There’s also a lot of argument about which one(s) are “right”, and to what extent the metrics agree with each others’ assessment of model correctness. Here we address one of the main arguments in this field (“regression vs RSA”) from the Weak-Strong Equivalence perspective. (See series Part 1 for a refresher on Weak-Strong equivalence.)

Contents

  1. The RSA vs linear regression debate

  2. Decomposing RSMs into core and noise terms.

  3. Connection to behavior and mechanism

  4. Canonical RSA and weak-strong equivalence

  5. The RSA-ridge relationship

  6. Neural sampling is “symmetry-Like noise”

  7. Does the choice of metric matter? Revisited.

1. The RSA vs Linear Regression debate

Two of the main metrics the NeuroAI community uses are:

  1. Linear regression similarity (basically the same as “weak alignment” in earlier posts in this series). Linear regression similarity metrics come in a number of flavors, but they all basically work by (a) fitting a linear map between source and target using some training set; (b) measuring per-unit (neuron/voxel) prediction accuracy on held-out stimuli; and (c) reporting an average over units.

  2. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). RSA also comes in a number of flavors, but basically works by computing, for each feature set, a Representational Similarity Matrix (RSM) — that is, a NxN matrix of correlations between feature vectors, where N is the number of stimuli. (The features can come from either neural data or model activations.) The (i,j)-th entry of the RSM is a similarity measure: it’s 1 if the feature set “thinks” stimulus i and stimulus j are essentially the same. The whole RSM is like a layout across all the stimuli of which stimuli the feature set “thinks” are relatively similar to each other and which are not, which is why the RSM is sometimes called the “representational geometry”. Two feature generators are compared by correlating their RSMs (thought of as long flattened-out vectors); the output of this comparison is the RSA score between two representations, which is high (close to 1.0) whenever two feature sets basically make the same default judgements about which stimuli are similar/different.

Each of these metrics has surface-level pros and cons. Regression similarity can lead to high prediction power (which is useful for practical purposes), since it optimizes a bunch of parameters (the regression weights) explicitly to improve predictions. By the same token, regression needs quite a bit of data to fit the regression parameters well. Conversely, RSA doesn’t need to estimate any additional parameters (and so can be useful in low-data regimes). But by the same token, RSA might underestimate the latent representational capacity that could be extracted from a set of features by a downstream interpreter that has the ability do some reweighting (such as a real neuronal “readout” might do).

But this direct accounting of practical pros and cons doesn’t really capture a deeper issue about metric choice in NeuroAI. A major question (maybe you could even say “controversy”) that has arisen in the field asks something like:

“Which metric is more the right way to compare candidate models to neural data for the purposes of true understanding? Is there a tradeoff between maximizing prediction accuracy and achieving scientific meaning?”

With this issue in mind, let’s dive into what the new version of the Contravariance Theory paper tells us about RSA and its relation to linear regression. (For all the gory math details see §A.12 of the paper’s appendix. Also see §A.13 for a similar treatment of another popular metric, Centered Kernel Analysis (CKA).)

2. Decomposing RSMs into core and noise terms.

Much of our thinking about RSA in the Contravariance Theory paper is built on recent work from Theiß, Braun, Saxe, and Grant, entitled Parameter symmetries determine representational geometry in overparameterized nonlinear networks, from here referred to as [TBSG].

The first main result of [TBSG] is that RSMs decompose into two parts1:

where:

  • the qj factors are computed from the privileged axes,

  • the 𝛾j factors are controlled by reweightings and multiplicity of the privileged axes, and as such do not affect the downstream computations, and

  • the a matrix is determined only by function-preserving symmetries that are irrelevant to the represented function. Theiß et al call the a matrix “noise”, because it’s entirely composed of nuisance degrees of freedom.

The [TBSG] decomposition has two major consequences.

First, the “raw” RSM can be totally dominated by factors that are independent of functionality. Indeed, the 𝛾j values and a matrix can be chosen so that two representations with identical privileged axes (and thus identical qj factors) can have arbitrarily different RSMs — e.g. be arbitrarily far apart under the RSA metric — even though they compute the same downstream function. These factors can obscure or even dominate the part of the RSM that reflects the features actually used in the computation. They are “functionally silent but geometrically visible”.

Second, the RSM has a uniquely-determined core geometry that is task linked, and where perturbations to that geometry would have substantial consequences on the downstream represented function. To get at that core geometry, one needs to remove the a matrix and normalize out the 𝛾j factors — that is one needs to canonicalize.

Key implication for NeuroAI (from [TSBG]): Raw representational geometry is very sensitive to factors that don’t really matter for the computation. However, there is a unique core geometry present in every feature set that is task-linked.

3. Connection to Behavior and Mechanism

The above result has a key conceptual implication for contravariance. Recall from Parts 1 and 2 of this series that in the hard task-constrained regime, linear similarity is both connected to lower-level mechanistic structure recorded in the privileged axes (Weak-Strong Equivalence), and highly constrained by the task (through Zippering). However, as we’ve just seen, RSA can be dominated by task- and privileged axis-irrelevant factors. Thus, we should predict that RSA similarity will in general be less correlated across trained neural network models than ridge similarity with other factors that themselves do depend on the core computation — such as downstream behavior (e.g. task error patterns) or upstream privileged axes metrics (e.g. V1 unit tuning-curves) .

Key prediction for NeuroAI: RSA should be a less good predictor of behavioral and mechanistic metrics than ridge similarity, in the task-constraining model regime. The nuisance factors will get in RSA’s way.

See Part 4b: RSA empirics for an investigation of this prediction from an empirical viewpoint.

4. Canonical RSA and Weak-Strong Equivalence

Canonicalization is a process by which the task-irrelevant factors are removed to reveal the core geometry. In the Contravariance Theory paper appendix §A.12.5, we describe two ways to do this:

Privileged-Axis Normalized RSM: First, you can work directly with the privileged axes, ensure only one copy of each privileged axis type is used, and divide by its norm, before computing the RSM. More formally, for each privileged axis fj, define the normalized RSM component for that axis by

(this is an a NxN matrix, where N is the number of stimuli) and, assuming there are m preferred axes, define the axis-normalized canonical RSM by:

In words, this makes each essential feature’s response profile unit length, gives each essential axis one copy and equal weight, and computes the usual RSM of that canonicalized representation.

Minimum-Norm Balanced RSM: Unlike the axis-normalized idea above, in [TBSG] a more sensitive (but complicated) approach is taken: instead of discarding axis weights, [TBSG] describe procedures for choosing specific weightings that depend on the size or cost of a generated feature and on the downstream readout that it uses, rather than giving every essential class one equal vote as RSMax does. There are multiple cost functions that make sense, including minimum representation (MR) and minimum weight (MW) costs (see the original [TBSG] paper for details). Such weightings attempt to take biological implementation costs into account: MR might approximate activity/metabolic cost, while MW might approximate synaptic or wiring cost.

Whether one prefers the axis-normalized or minimum-norm versions depends on one’s purposes: if one just cares about “the computation”, the former is more appropriate; while if one is interested in “the biophysics”, the latter may be more on target.

The key point with respect to contravariance for RSA is that, regardless of which canonicalization method one picks, canonical RSA obeys Weak-Strong equivalence, unlike raw RSA. That is:

Theorem (informal): In the hard-task context, if two same-architecture networks A and B are linearly aligned at two adjacent layers l and l+1 then they have matching canonical RSMs at the earlier layer:

(See the Contravariance Paper appendix §A.12.5 for formal mathematical details.)

We can also show a soft version of this that relates defects in linear alignment to small mismatches in canonoical RSA, just as with privileged axes (see Part 1 of this series for a refresher on those results). Similarly, a full zippering result follows for RSA as well (see Part 2 for more on zippering).

Key implication for NeuroAI: By focusing on the core task-relevant geometry, canonical RSA restores the contravariance-theory link between function and representation in the hard-task context.

5. The RSA-Ridge relationship

Given that RSA and Ridge are both standard metrics, it is worth understanding what their relationship is.

After canonicalizing to reveal the core geometry (either method is ok), it turns out that there is a very simple relationship:

for some constant C. The funny ≾ symbol means that the relationship is a frontier, rather than a strict equality, but that under reasonable conditions, the equality is close to being achieved. (See the Contravariance paper appendix §A.12.6 for the math details on how this is shown.)

This relationship means that if you plot canonical RSA (x-axis) vs ridge score (y-axis), you should see a scatter plot that looks roughly like a square root relationship:

On the left, I’m plotting a schematic canonical RSA-vs-ridge relationship. On the right, I’m plotting a schematic for raw RSA-vs-ridge. There, a square-root relationship might exist to some extent (depending on how bad the effect of the nuisance variables are), but it will be a bit more obscured and perhaps in some cases entirely absent. See Part 4b: RSA empirics, for more on this topic from an empirical viewpoint.

6. Neural sampling is “symmetry-like” noise.

Neuroscience experiments are, and have always been, heavily affected by issues of undersampling or biased sampling.

In classic old-school single-electrode electrophysiology experiments, only one or a small number of neurons were explored at a time, with perhaps a few tens of neurons experimentally tested in a series of separate recording sessions, over the course of an experiment. This sampling sparseness was exacerbated by a strong bias in stimulus sampling, since neurons were identified for recording in the first place (during the process of lowering the electrode through cortex) by virtue of their ability to respond to a specific test stimulus set, so neurons not excited by that set might be just ignored.

Array electrophysiology improved this by allowing hundreds of units to be recorded simultaneously for tens of thousands of stimuli, and reduced the stimulus-biased localization problem. Nonetheless, even the largest array electrophysiology datasets only record several thousand out of tens of millions of units in an area, sampled in a highly spatially non-uniform fashion.

Though fMRI has full coverage, it too has strong non-uniformity in signal strength across the cortex, leading to complex spatial biases and distortions in response patterns. Other neuroscience measurement modalities (Ca2+ imaging, ECoG, &c) have related issues at different scales.

Moreover, these effects are especially important when tuning is itself spatially organized, as it is in many real brain areas. A spatially localized sample from such a system is therefore not merely a smaller statistically-equivalent subset of the full system: it is biased toward the functions represented in that part of the cortical sheet.

The key point for us here is that the effect on RSA of different kinds of sampling biases are analogous to the same nuisance parameters discussed above. In fact, spatial bias is the measurement version of the [TBSG] ambiguities: the same underlying computation and the same privileged axes can yield different raw RSMs because experimental biases assign them different effective scales, multiplicities, and mixtures.

The effects are summarized in the following table:

Some of these effects are mitigated by canonical RSA, but not all. It can help with recording gain, e.g. when the same response profile is multiplied by a scalar; or with exact multiplicity, e.g. if one identifiable tuning/axis class is recorded several times on one side and fewer times on the other. For example, if two arrays both observe orientation and color axes, but one records many near-copies of the orientation axis, an axis quotient could—in principle, after identifying that class—properly count orientation once rather than according to the number of recorded copies. But it will not mitigate the main spatial-sampling problems, such as:

  • a localized array missing whole functional patches;

  • topographic sampling changing which distinct feature axes are represented;

  • fMRI distortions mixing nearby axes;

  • or finite sampling omitting rare axes.

So, you know, nullius in verba &c . . .

Key implication for NeuroAI: An unavoidable issue with neural experiments — sampling — strongly affects the raw RSA measure, and the outcomes mimic the effects of computation-irrelevant symmetries. Canonicalization can only partially mitigate this, but ridge similarity should be more sampling-stable.

See Part 4b: RSA empirics for further data-driven investigation of this point.

Does the choice of metric matter?, revisited.

[FYI: though I haven’t described it here, b/c this post is already long enough, the Contravariance Theory paper §A.13 treats the CKA metric, finding very similar results to the RSA situation.]

Despite taking a certain amount of flak on social media (and probably quite a bit more behind closed doors) for making the claim in an earlier post that perhaps the choice of metric didn’t matter all that much (because weak equivalence established that a strong and a weak metric were actually pretty similar), I nonetheless mostly persist in this view, and see the RSA/CKA results as mostly reinforcing this outlook.

Basically, I interpret the above results as saying: canonical RSA/CKA comes along for the weak-strong equivalence ride with privileged-axis and linear alignment, and the non-canonical part of RSA/CKA should probably be discarded anyhow. Do you interpret things very differently?

1

In our Contravariance Theory paper appendix sections §§A.12.2-3, we slightly strengthen the [TBSG] result to show that the decomposition is unique and that the only symmetry factors that matter generically are the duplications, additions, and scalings that the original [TBSG] paper identifies. Our results come at the cost of using a slightly stronger notion of minimality (rather than their irreducibility), but that is consistent with the other conditions deployed in the Contravariance Theory paper.

items.title: Contravariance Theory, Part 3: Transformers!
items.description: In which we explore zippering and privileged axes for the transformer circuit.
items.content:
(This is Part 3 of a series on Contravariance Theory. See Part 0 to get the big picture.)

Transformers are the dominant microcircuit architecture of AI, due to their robust learning and generalization capacities. How they might relate to neurons is an open question, but regardless of the resolution of that thorny topic, any theory of the Contravariance Principle in DNNs would be incomplete without a treatment of the transformer circuit.

Here we do a deep dive on that topic, presenting a (hopefully!) reader-friendly version of the material discussed in appendix section §A.8 of the Contravariance Theory paper. The answer is pretty interesting!

All transformers are divided into three parts — one of which is the residual stream, the MLP block is another, and what is called in the language of machine learning the attention block, the third.1 It turns out these behave somewhat differently with respect to contravariance. Specifically:

  • Weak-Strong Equivalence (WSE) happens for the MLP and attention blocks. WSE is the local phenomenon in which, under hard-task constraints, weak linear alignment at neighboring layers converts into strong axis (or transformer head) alignment. (See Part 1 of this series for a refresher on WSE.)

  • … but the residual stream is different. WSE does not happen for the residual stream. There is an uncontrolled parameter space in each residual connection that destroys privileged axes there.

  • We find that Zippering occurs in the residual stream of transformers. Zippering is the global phenomenon in which, under hard-task and minimality constraints, weak alignment at a downstream layer cascades upstream through a network, providing the core mechanism of the Contravariance Principle. (See Part 2 of this series for a refresher on Zippering.)

  • The above two results combine to imply that there are privileged representational axes throughout transformer hierarchies! . . . but you can’t look in the residual stream to find them.

See below for a detailed account of each of these ideas.

A graphical representation of the situation of contravariance for transformers. In the image, A and B are two networks being compared. We find that (i) Weak Zippering obtains for the residual stream and (ii) Weak-Strong Equivalence obtains for the MLP block in the usual way, and modulo “head-gauges” for the attention block. Privileged axes thus arise in the MLP and attention blocks, but not in the residual stream.

The Transformer circuit has three parts.

To establish basic background and common terms, we distinguish three parts within the transformer circuit:

  • the attention block (red in the diagram above) is the component of the transformer circuit in which inputs are mixed using a learnable pairwise multiplicative operation,

  • the MLP block (green) is the portion in which inputs are mixed using a short linear-nonlinear cascade,

  • the residual stream (blue) of the transformer combines the MLP and attention blocks additively and passes forward to the next layer.

Much ink has been spilled in discussing the functional implications of these structural components, but I will note here one reasonable (imo) interpretation: that the MLP block and residual stream support a linear representation of entities, and that the attention block supports efficient detection of relationships between entities.

The Residual Stream Supports Zippering. . .

At a global level within the network, the key observation is that the transformer residual stream supports zippering. The reason for this is essentially the same as why regular affine-nonlinear (e.g. ReLU) networks support zippering (see Part 2): that if your network is minimal (informally, not wasting units and layers), all solutions are either a single canonical solution, or one of a set of “silly solutions” that pointlessly complicate the pathways relative to the unique minimal solution — but these silly solutions turn out to be very rare (that is, can be proven to be “measure zero” in the set of all networks).

To understand intuitively why this is, suppose two candidate networks became misaligned at one layer. The next layer’s nonlinearities turn that disagreement into new, visible differences; later nonlinearities generally create still more structure that must be reconciled. To ultimately arrive at the same terminal computation in a minimal way, all of those differences would have to be canceled with great precision (the “silly solution”). That high-precision cancelling is exceptional rather than common. So networks can in principle “wander apart in silly ways and then return to the real computation”, but doing so requires special tuning that is extremely unlikely to arise during real-world optimization.

Thus, a canonical solution (up to weak alignment) dominates at each layer of the hierarchy. The full mathematical formalization of this argument, which is a little bit more involved for the transformer circuit than for the simpler affine case, is in appendix sections §§A.8.4-5 of the Contravariance Theory paper.

These theoretical results are consistent with recent empirical work both in vision and LLMs. In vision, [Kapoor et al., 2025] show that hierarchical correspondences exist for transformers under the linear regression metric across distinct networks solving the same task (and actually for stricter metrics than linear as well, including Procrustes, permutation, and soft-matching). In language, across several dozen open-weight LLMs, layers at corresponding relative depths induce similar activation geometries [Wolfram and Schein, 2025].

. . . but NOT Weak-Strong Equivalence or privileged axes.

Interestingly, the residual stream of the transformer does NOT support the conversion of linear alignment on two adjacent layers into a set of preferred single-unit-level axis choices.

This is because, built into the very definition of the residual computation, is an arbitrary invertible affine change of basis that can mix the residual-stream coordinates without changing the Transformer’s computation. Imagine rewriting every residual vector in a new, thoroughly mixed coordinate system. As long as every attention and MLP operation is adjusted to read from and write to that new system, the Transformer computes exactly the same function. The residual stream of the original and rewritten transformer are then perfectly linearly related, even though no individual coordinate in one corresponds to an individual coordinate in the other.

This observation is consistent with the interesting empirical observation from [Kapoor et al., 2025] finding a lack of privileged axes in transformers.

There should be privileged axes in the other blocks.

Residual streams therefore only zipper weakly—they contain the same state up to an affine change of coordinates—without their native axes aligning strongly. But, interestingly, the trivial mixing construction that instantly destroys canonical axis bases in the residual stream does not apply to the other branches of the transformer.

The key difference is where the coordinate change sits relative to the nonlinearity:

  • For the MLP block: MLP layers are different from the residual stream because each hidden coordinate is passed separately through the ReLU. A dense mixing of the coordinates before that operation cannot easily be fully undone afterward if the gates are truly used by the network to solve the task. This is just the same argument as “regular” zippering/Weak-strong Equivalence. (See Part 1 of this series.)

  • For the attention block: the residual-stream privileged axis-destroying argument actually does partially apply. The query/key (q/k) space and value/output (v/o) space can each be changed by an arbitrary invertible basis transformation without changing the head, just like the residual stream. HOWEVER: for the head as a functional unit, arbitrarily blending two heads does not trivially compute the same function as the original heads. In fact, under minimality assumptions, each distinct head turns out to generically have a unique identifiable role. As a result, Weak-Strong Equivalence applies. The formal math behind this conclusion is shown in §A.8.1 of the Contravariance Theory paper.

There hasn’t been a ton of empirical work verifying these ideas, especially in vision networks, so this is a frontier for future empirical NeuroAI research. One observation from LLMs that would seem to be consistent with these ideas is the whole collection of “biology of LLM circuits” interpretability results suggesting that specific attention heads reliably take on certain roles. Clarifying the connection between LLM interpretability and the privileged attention heads predicted by the contravariance theory is also a natural area for future research.

So how similar are ViTs and CNNs?

The theoretical results don’t explicit say that two networks of apparently different architectures solving the same task have to end up being similar, either up to weak (linear) or strong (privileged axis) equivalence. But they do kind of raise the question: to what extent do the ideas that allow for proving weak-strong equivalence and zippering suggest that similar structures will appear across architecture types? How similar are the linear spans and privileged axes in corresponding-ish layers of CNNs and Vision Transformers (ViTs)? Are there corresponding-ish layers in the first place? After all, even though ViTs seem on the surface like they’re very different from CNNs, the ViT class and the CNN class could in principle learn similar functions after optimization for a common task. This is a great set of questions for future investigation.

Key implication for NeuroAI: Transformers are similar to “regular” deep neural networks in their contravariance behavior, but only have privileged axes in some parts of the circuit. These are the places to look for characteristic neural signatures.
